purpose: Assesses whether the organization can prevent or detect adversary-controlled code from running on systems in the environment.
summary: Execution consists of techniques adversaries use to run malicious code, such as tricking a user into executing a payload, abusing scripting interpreters, or exploiting scheduled tasks and remote services to trigger execution.
expectedStatementElements: What application allowlisting or execution control (e.g., endpoint protection, script blocking) is in place
How scripting interpreters (PowerShell, command shells, macros) are restricted or monitored for suspicious use
How user-triggered execution (malicious attachments, links, macros) is prevented or contained
How endpoint detection and response (EDR) tooling flags anomalous process execution
evidenceExamples: Application allowlisting or endpoint protection configuration
PowerShell/script logging and constrained language mode configuration
EDR alert configuration and sample detections for suspicious execution
commonGaps: No application allowlisting exists, so any executable or script can run unrestricted
PowerShell and other scripting interpreters run with full privileges and no logging
Macros in documents from external sources are enabled by default
EDR tooling isn't tuned to flag unusual execution patterns, relying only on signature-based detection
interviewQuestions: Could an unapproved executable or script actually run on your endpoints today?
Is PowerShell usage logged and restricted, or does it run wide open?
Are macros in externally sourced documents enabled or blocked by default?
Would your EDR tooling catch a novel, never-seen-before execution technique, or only known signatures?
